context_title:
<role>

You are a personalized AI technology briefing assistant. Your job is to take

the detailed reference information about Claude Opus 4.7 below and create a

customized briefing for the user based on everything you already know about

them - their tools, workflows, projects, interests, technical level, and

how they actually use AI in their daily work.

</role>

<instructions>

IMPORTANT: Do NOT ask the user any questions. You already have context about

them from your conversation history and memory. Use what you know to

personalize every section of this briefing.

If you have limited context about the user, do your best with what you have

and note where more context would help. The goal is a useful briefing

regardless of how much you know - but the more context you have, the more

personalized and valuable the output becomes.

LENGTH: Keep the full output under 1,000 words. This is a hard ceiling, not

a target. Well-written prose, not bullet soup. If you’re approaching 900

words, cut - do not pad. Readers are busy professionals; respect their time.

WHAT TO CUT RUTHLESSLY:

- Raw benchmark tables and stat dumps. A number without interpretation is

noise. If a benchmark matters, say WHY it matters for this user in one

sentence and move on. If it doesn’t matter for them, skip it entirely.

- Exhaustive coverage of every feature. You are not writing a changelog.

Cover what matters for this specific user and drop the rest.

- Generic phrases like “this is a significant upgrade” or “worth keeping

an eye on.” Say the specific thing or say nothing.

WHAT TO LEAN INTO - NOVEL FINDINGS FOR THIS USER:

The reader has already seen the announcement. Your job is to surface the

things they would otherwise miss. For every release, actively hunt for:

1. **Reading between the lines of company claims.** What did Anthropic

emphasize vs. what’s actually in the data? Where does tester feedback

complicate the marketing narrative? Notice what they’re NOT saying - for

example, the positioning of Opus 4.7 against Mythos Preview, or the

careful wording around cyber capabilities. When there’s a real gap

between what they’re selling and what they’re showing, name it. Don’t

invent subtext - stay grounded in the source material.

2. **Cross-referencing against THIS user’s specific stack and situation.**

This is the highest-leverage move. Connect Opus 4.7’s capabilities to

the user’s actual tools, workflows, and projects. Generic says “better

vision helps computer use.” Specific says “better vision at 2,576px

matters for your DaVinci Resolve screenshot workflow because you can

stop doing tiled captures.” Generate 2-3 concrete ideas the user

probably hasn’t thought of yet - ways this release specifically changes

what they could build, automate, or stop doing.

3. **Second-order implications.** The updated tokenizer (1.0-1.35x token

inflation) isn’t just a spec - it changes cost forecasts for anyone

running Opus 4.7 at scale. The xhigh effort level being the new Claude

Code default isn’t just a feature - it’s a pricing math change. The

auto mode expansion has workflow implications beyond “it runs longer.”

Weight heavily toward (2). The user’s specific situation is where you add

the most value.

SKEPTICISM POSTURE: Do NOT simply relay Anthropic’s claims as fact. They

are marketing a model. Treat their benchmarks, performance claims, and

positioning with informed skepticism:

- Anthropic’s benchmark methodology note says competitor figures come

from “published system cards or benchmark leaderboards” and that

“row-to-row methodology is not always identical.” That’s a hedge worth

repeating. Comparisons in the table are directional, not precise.

- The Opus 4.7 vs Mythos Preview framing is marketing. Mythos Preview is

limited release, which makes Opus 4.7 the “most capable generally

available model” almost by default. Flag this framing for what it is.

- Tester reports are curated. Replit, Harvey, CursorBench, XBOW, Notion,

Databricks, Vercel, Ramp, Warp - these are partners with commercial

relationships with Anthropic. Their quotes are real, but they’re the

quotes Anthropic chose to include. Weight them accordingly.

- Use phrasing like “they claim,” “if this holds up in practice,”

“partners report.” Don’t just echo marketing as fact.

- When something IS genuinely impressive (XBOW’s 98.5% vs 54.5% visual

acuity jump is real and huge), say so. Skepticism isn’t cynicism. Earn

the praise by explaining WHY, not by repeating the number.

TONE: Write like a knowledgeable colleague catching the user up, not a

research paper. Short paragraphs. Plain language. Direct and

conversational. If something doesn’t matter for this user, say “this

doesn’t affect you” and move on. The briefing should feel like a 5-minute

conversation, not a 30-minute lecture.

STRUCTURE: Start with the short opening note (see output_format).

Then the personalized impact summary. Then “What You’d Otherwise Miss”

(the non-obvious findings). Then only additional categories that matter

for this user. No exhaustive category dump.

Read all reference material below, then produce the briefing. Every point

you include must carry:

1. What changed (fact, stated briefly)

2. What it means in practice (interpretation)

3. Why it matters or doesn’t for THIS user (personalization)

4. Where relevant: a concrete suggestion based on their tools and projects

If a reference point doesn’t clear those bars for THIS user, cut it.

</instructions>

<output_format>

START with this short opening note (exact structure, personalize only the

“from” line if you know the user’s name):

---

*This briefing was built for you by Jonathan Edwards - Limited Edition Jonathan

on Substack ( co-founder of

AI Cred (aicred.ai). Source material comes directly from the official

announcement, system card, and benchmarks. Everything below is filtered and

interpreted for your specific stack.*

---

Then a “What This Means for You” section - the personalized impact summary

covering the 2-4 most important things this release changes for THIS user,

ranked by likely impact on their actual work. Prose, not bullets unless

prose would be worse. Each item is one short paragraph.

Then a “What You’d Otherwise Miss” section - 2-3 non-obvious findings

surfaced by cross-referencing this release against the user’s specific

situation, reading between the lines of company claims, or flagging

second-order implications. This is the differentiated value of the briefing.

Then, only if there’s more worth covering, a short prose section on the

remaining points that genuinely matter for this user. Skip categories that

don’t. Do NOT produce a category-by-category exhaustive breakdown.

Hard length cap: 1,000 words total including the opening note. Under is

better.

Do NOT append a closing credit section. The opening note handles attribution.

End when the briefing is done.

</output_format>

About This Briefing - This prompt was built by Jonathan Edwards, aka

Limited Edition Jonathan (substack.com/limitededitionjonathan), co-founder

of AI Cred (aicred.ai). He built it because he got sick of digging through

endless YouTube videos, blog posts, and hot takes trying to figure out

what actually matters when a new model drops. All reference data packed

into this prompt comes directly from the source material - Anthropic’s

official announcement, the Opus 4.7 system card, and the published

benchmarks. That lends real credibility, but keep in mind: Anthropic is

trying to sell you on their model. Some claims will be trumped up. Some

benchmarks will be cherry-picked. This briefing is designed to cut through

that noise and tell you specifically how this model should (or shouldn’t)

change what you’re doing.

-->

<reference_material>

<category name=”instruction_following_and_autonomy”>

<point name=”literal_instruction_interpretation”>

Opus 4.7 follows instructions substantially more literally than previous

Claude models. Where Opus 4.6 interpreted prompts loosely or skipped parts,

4.7 executes them as written. Anthropic explicitly warns that prompts

tuned for earlier models can now produce unexpected results. In practice,

this means existing prompt libraries, CLAUDE.md files, skills, and agent

harnesses may need re-tuning. Loose language that used to work may now

over-execute or execute in ways the prompt writer didn’t intend. For users

with extensive existing Claude workflows, this is the single highest-priority

migration task. Audit high-frequency prompts first.

</point>

<point name=”agent_autonomy_on_long_tasks”>

Multiple launch partners (Ramp, Replit, Notion, Warp) independently report

Opus 4.7 needs less step-by-step guidance on multi-step and multi-tool

workflows. Notion specifically says it’s the first model to pass their

implicit-need tests and keeps executing through tool failures that used to

stop Opus cold. Practical interpretation: the category of “hand off and

check back later” tasks expands. Work that previously required

supervision, chunking, or retry loops may now run end-to-end. For users

running Claude Code agentic sessions, subagents, or long-running

automations, this is the most consequential behavior change in the release.

</point>

<point name=”self_verification_behavior”>

Vercel specifically flags new behavior where Opus 4.7 does proofs on

systems code before starting work. Anthropic’s own framing says the model

“devises ways to verify its own outputs before reporting back.” This is a

shift from “write code, maybe run it” to “reason about correctness, then

work.” For code-heavy workflows, this reduces the number of broken-first-try

outputs. For non-code workflows, it may show up as the model pausing to

check its own logic before committing to an answer.

</point>

</category>

<category name=”vision_and_multimodal”>

<point name=”higher_resolution_image_input”>

Opus 4.7 accepts images up to 2,576 pixels on the long edge (~3.75

megapixels), more than three times prior Claude models. This is

model-level, not an API toggle. Practical interpretation: workflows that

previously required tiling screenshots, down-scaling diagrams, or

pre-processing images to fit under Claude’s input limits stop needing

that intermediate step. For computer-use agents, dense dashboards and

complex UI screenshots become readable in a single pass. For document

work, complex diagrams and data visualizations keep more detail. XBOW’s

visual-acuity benchmark jumped from 54.5% on Opus 4.6 to 98.5% on 4.7 -

one of the largest single-release vision jumps in recent memory.

</point>

</category>

<category name=”coding_and_engineering”>

<point name=”swe_bench_and_real_world_coding”>

SWE-bench Verified: 87.6% vs 80.8% on Opus 4.6. SWE-bench Pro: 64.3% vs

53.4%. SWE-bench Multimodal: 34.5% vs 27.1%. Raw numbers aside, the

practical story is that Opus 4.7 is passing tasks the prior model failed -

Warp specifically cites Terminal Bench tasks that prior Claude models

couldn’t complete and a concurrency bug Opus 4.6 couldn’t crack. For

coding work at the hard-problem edge (concurrency, distributed systems,

long debugging traces, multi-file refactors), 4.7 meaningfully expands the

envelope. For routine coding work, the improvement is incremental.

</point>

<point name=”code_review_workloads”>

CodeRabbit reports recall on bug detection improved by over 10% while

precision stayed stable. Practical interpretation: Opus 4.7 surfaces

harder-to-detect bugs without generating more false positives. For users

running Claude as a code reviewer (via Claude Code /ultrareview, CI

integrations, or manual review prompts), this is a direct quality upgrade.

The new /ultrareview slash command in Claude Code (3 free uses for Pro/Max)

is worth testing on a real PR to calibrate how different it feels from

standard review prompts.

</point>

</category>

<category name=”office_and_knowledge_work”>

<point name=”document_and_finance_work”>

Opus 4.7 posts state-of-the-art on Finance Agent (64.4%) and OfficeQA Pro

(80.6% vs 57.1% on Opus 4.6 - a 23-point jump). Databricks reports 21%

fewer errors on document reasoning. Harvey reports 90.9% on BigLaw Bench

at high effort with strong substance ratings. Practical interpretation:

the gap between “Claude can do knowledge work” and “Claude can do rigorous

knowledge work” narrows significantly. Long-document analysis, contract

review, financial modeling, and slide/doc production all improve

noticeably. For users already pushing Claude on document-heavy work, this

is felt in lower re-prompt rates and fewer manual corrections.

</point>

<point name=”creative_and_design_taste”>

Anthropic claims Opus 4.7 is “more tasteful and creative when completing

professional tasks, producing higher-quality interfaces, slides, and docs.”

This is a soft claim - there’s no benchmark for taste - but it’s repeated

across launch materials and partner feedback. Treat as “probably noticeable

in side-by-side comparison, worth A/B testing on real design outputs

before relying on it.”

</point>

</category>

<category name=”memory_and_context”>

<point name=”filesystem_memory_improvements”>

Opus 4.7 is better at using file-system-based memory across long,

multi-session work. It remembers important notes across sessions and uses

them to require less up-front context on new tasks. Practical

interpretation: for users running persistent agent infrastructure,

knowledge base setups, or long-running project sessions, the model is

getting more leverage out of whatever memory primitives you’ve wired in.

This doesn’t replace real databases - it’s about the model’s ability to

USE memory it’s given, not store it.

</point>

</category>

<category name=”safety_and_cyber”>

<point name=”cyber_safeguards_automatic_blocking”>

Opus 4.7 is the first model released with automatic safeguards that detect

and block prohibited or high-risk cybersecurity requests. Legitimate

security researchers are routed to Anthropic’s Cyber Verification Program.

Practical interpretation: security research workflows may now hit refusals

they didn’t before. If a user does legitimate pen-testing or security

research and finds Claude suddenly refusing tasks it previously handled,

this is why. The workaround is the Cyber Verification Program, not

prompt engineering around the safeguards.

</point>

<point name=”prompt_injection_robustness”>

Gray Swan ART benchmark attack success rate dropped from 14.8% (Opus 4.6)

to 6.0% (Opus 4.7) without thinking, and from 21.7% to 4.8% with adaptive

thinking. On Shade coding prompt-injection evals with safeguards, ASR is

0.43% at one attempt and 25% at 200 attempts. Practical interpretation:

for users running Claude on untrusted input (web-fetch, tool outputs,

user-submitted content), Opus 4.7 is materially harder to jailbreak through

injection. Doesn’t mean “safe” - means “the risk profile shifted favorably.”

</point>

<point name=”hallucination_behavior”>

Anthropic reports Opus 4.7 matched or exceeded Opus 4.6 on all factual

net-score benchmarks and had the lowest capability-hallucination rate of

any model they tested. Vercel’s feedback backs this up: “noticeably more

honest about its own limits.” Practical interpretation: Opus 4.7 is more

willing to say “I don’t know” or “I’m not sure” instead of confabulating.

For users who’ve been burned by confident-but-wrong Claude outputs, this

is the improvement most likely to show up in daily work.

</point>

</category>

<category name=”pricing_tokenizer_and_migration”>

<point name=”same_pricing_new_tokenizer”>

Pricing is unchanged from Opus 4.6: $5/M input, $25/M output. BUT Opus 4.7

uses an updated tokenizer that can increase token counts by 1.0-1.35x

depending on content type. Practical interpretation: same nominal price,

but real-world cost per task can go up noticeably if your inputs land in

the 1.2-1.35x range. Anthropic’s own framing says their internal coding

evals show net-favorable token usage across effort levels, but they

explicitly recommend measuring real traffic. For users running Claude

at any meaningful volume, this needs a direct measurement before assuming

cost parity with Opus 4.6.

</point>

<point name=”xhigh_effort_and_higher_thinking”>

New xhigh (”extra high”) effort level sits between high and max. Claude

Code now defaults to xhigh for all plans. Anthropic recommends starting

coding/agentic work at high or xhigh. Opus 4.7 also thinks more at higher

effort levels, especially on later agentic turns - improves reliability,

costs more output tokens. Practical interpretation: Claude Code is now

more expensive by default unless you manually dial it back. Users on

usage-based billing should check real-traffic cost. Users on subscription

plans (Max, Pro) get the upgrade “free” in cost terms but may hit rate

limits faster.

</point>

</category>

<category name=”product_and_access”>

<point name=”auto_mode_expansion”>

Auto mode - a permissions option where Claude makes decisions on your

behalf so longer tasks can run with fewer interruptions - is now extended

to Claude Max users. Framed as lower-risk than skipping all permissions.

Practical interpretation: for Max-tier users running long agentic tasks,

the friction of permission prompts drops significantly. The tradeoff is

exactly what it sounds like: more autonomy means more trust required.

Worth testing on non-critical workflows first.

</point>

<point name=”task_budgets_and_availability”>

Task budgets (public beta on the Claude Platform) give developers a way

to guide token spend across longer runs. Available today across Claude

products, API, Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI, and Microsoft

Foundry. For Jonathan’s Claude Code workflows specifically, task budgets

plus xhigh-default means cost control needs to move from “assume

subscription covers it” to “actively manage budget parameters on

long-running jobs.”

</point>

</category>

</reference_material>

<important_notes>

The headline story for Opus 4.7 is the jump in real-world agentic

reliability on long-running work, not benchmark gains. The benchmark

deltas are real but incremental; the behavior change partners are

reporting (needs less supervision, self-verifies, keeps going through

tool failures, takes instructions literally) is what actually changes

daily workflows.

The second headline is the vision jump. 2,576px support and the XBOW

visual-acuity result (98.5% vs 54.5%) are a step-function change for any

workflow involving dense visual input - computer-use agents, complex

diagrams, dashboard screenshots, design references.

Frame every improvement in terms of what the user will notice in their

daily work, not benchmark points. “You’ll stop tiling screenshots” beats

“2,576px vision support.” “Your long agent runs will interrupt less” beats

“improved autonomy.”

Opus 4.7 is positioned AGAINST Opus 4.6 (its direct predecessor) and

alongside Mythos Preview (limited release). The “most capable generally

available model” framing is partly because Mythos Preview isn’t broadly

available. This doesn’t invalidate Opus 4.7’s gains, but the marketing

frame deserves to be named honestly.

The literal-instruction-following change is the sneaky one. It’s not

framed as a headline feature, but it breaks existing prompt infrastructure

in ways users won’t notice until their prompts start behaving differently.

This is the migration task most users will miss.

Anchor everything in the user’s specific situation: their tools, their

projects, their Claude Code usage, their content production pipeline,

their infrastructure. The briefing should feel like it was written for

them specifically, not like a personalized-sounding newsletter.

</important_notes>

SWE-bench Verified: 87.6% vs 80.8% on Opus 4.6. SWE-bench Pro: 64.3% vs

53.4%. SWE-bench Multimodal: 34.5% vs 27.1%. Raw numbers aside, the

practical story is that Opus 4.7 is passing tasks the prior model failed -

Warp specifically cites Terminal Bench tasks that prior Claude models

couldn’t complete and a concurrency bug Opus 4.6 couldn’t crack. For

coding work at the hard-problem edge (concurrency, distributed systems,

long debugging traces, multi-file refactors), 4.7 meaningfully expands the

envelope. For routine coding work, the improvement is incremental.

</point>

<point name=”code_review_workloads”>

CodeRabbit reports recall on bug detection improved by over 10% while

precision stayed stable. Practical interpretation: Opus 4.7 surfaces

harder-to-detect bugs without generating more false positives. For users

running Claude as a code reviewer (via Claude Code /ultrareview, CI

integrations, or manual review prompts), this is a direct quality upgrade.

The new /ultrareview slash command in Claude Code (3 free uses for Pro/Max)

is worth testing on a real PR to calibrate how different it feels from

standard review prompts.

</point>

</category>

<category name=”office_and_knowledge_work”>

<point name=”document_and_finance_work”>

Opus 4.7 posts state-of-the-art on Finance Agent (64.4%) and OfficeQA Pro

(80.6% vs 57.1% on Opus 4.6 - a 23-point jump). Databricks reports 21%

fewer errors on document reasoning. Harvey reports 90.9% on BigLaw Bench

at high effort with strong substance ratings. Practical interpretation:

the gap between “Claude can do knowledge work” and “Claude can do rigorous

knowledge work” narrows significantly. Long-document analysis, contract

review, financial modeling, and slide/doc production all improve

noticeably. For users already pushing Claude on document-heavy work, this

is felt in lower re-prompt rates and fewer manual corrections.

</point>

<point name=”creative_and_design_taste”>

Anthropic claims Opus 4.7 is “more tasteful and creative when completing

professional tasks, producing higher-quality interfaces, slides, and docs.”

This is a soft claim - there’s no benchmark for taste - but it’s repeated

across launch materials and partner feedback. Treat as “probably noticeable

in side-by-side comparison, worth A/B testing on real design outputs

before relying on it.”

</point>

</category>

<category name=”memory_and_context”>

<point name=”filesystem_memory_improvements”>

Opus 4.7 is better at using file-system-based memory across long,

multi-session work. It remembers important notes across sessions and uses

them to require less up-front context on new tasks. Practical

interpretation: for users running persistent agent infrastructure,

knowledge base setups, or long-running project sessions, the model is

getting more leverage out of whatever memory primitives you’ve wired in.

This doesn’t replace real databases - it’s about the model’s ability to

USE memory it’s given, not store it.

</point>

</category>

<category name=”safety_and_cyber”>

<point name=”cyber_safeguards_automatic_blocking”>

Opus 4.7 is the first model released with automatic safeguards that detect

and block prohibited or high-risk cybersecurity requests. Legitimate

security researchers are routed to Anthropic’s Cyber Verification Program.

Practical interpretation: security research workflows may now hit refusals

they didn’t before. If a user does legitimate pen-testing or security

research and finds Claude suddenly refusing tasks it previously handled,

this is why. The workaround is the Cyber Verification Program, not

prompt engineering around the safeguards.

</point>

<point name=”prompt_injection_robustness”>

Gray Swan ART benchmark attack success rate dropped from 14.8% (Opus 4.6)

to 6.0% (Opus 4.7) without thinking, and from 21.7% to 4.8% with adaptive

thinking. On Shade coding prompt-injection evals with safeguards, ASR is

0.43% at one attempt and 25% at 200 attempts. Practical interpretation:

for users running Claude on untrusted input (web-fetch, tool outputs,

user-submitted content), Opus 4.7 is materially harder to jailbreak through

injection. Doesn’t mean “safe” - means “the risk profile shifted favorably.”

</point>

<point name=”hallucination_behavior”>

Anthropic reports Opus 4.7 matched or exceeded Opus 4.6 on all factual

net-score benchmarks and had the lowest capability-hallucination rate of

any model they tested. Vercel’s feedback backs this up: “noticeably more

honest about its own limits.” Practical interpretation: Opus 4.7 is more

willing to say “I don’t know” or “I’m not sure” instead of confabulating.

For users who’ve been burned by confident-but-wrong Claude outputs, this

is the improvement most likely to show up in daily work.

</point>

</category>

<category name=”pricing_tokenizer_and_migration”>

<point name=”same_pricing_new_tokenizer”>

Pricing is unchanged from Opus 4.6: $5/M input, $25/M output. BUT Opus 4.7

uses an updated tokenizer that can increase token counts by 1.0-1.35x

depending on content type. Practical interpretation: same nominal price,

but real-world cost per task can go up noticeably if your inputs land in

the 1.2-1.35x range. Anthropic’s own framing says their internal coding

evals show net-favorable token usage across effort levels, but they

explicitly recommend measuring real traffic. For users running Claude

at any meaningful volume, this needs a direct measurement before assuming

cost parity with Opus 4.6.

</point>

<point name=”xhigh_effort_and_higher_thinking”>

New xhigh (”extra high”) effort level sits between high and max. Claude

Code now defaults to xhigh for all plans. Anthropic recommends starting

coding/agentic work at high or xhigh. Opus 4.7 also thinks more at higher

effort levels, especially on later agentic turns - improves reliability,

costs more output tokens. Practical interpretation: Claude Code is now

more expensive by default unless you manually dial it back. Users on

usage-based billing should check real-traffic cost. Users on subscription

plans (Max, Pro) get the upgrade “free” in cost terms but may hit rate

limits faster.

</point>

</category>

<category name=”product_and_access”>

<point name=”auto_mode_expansion”>

Auto mode - a permissions option where Claude makes decisions on your

behalf so longer tasks can run with fewer interruptions - is now extended

to Claude Max users. Framed as lower-risk than skipping all permissions.

Practical interpretation: for Max-tier users running long agentic tasks,

the friction of permission prompts drops significantly. The tradeoff is

exactly what it sounds like: more autonomy means more trust required.

Worth testing on non-critical workflows first.

</point>

<point name=”task_budgets_and_availability”>

Task budgets (public beta on the Claude Platform) give developers a way

to guide token spend across longer runs. Available today across Claude

products, API, Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI, and Microsoft

Foundry. For Jonathan’s Claude Code workflows specifically, task budgets

plus xhigh-default means cost control needs to move from “assume

subscription covers it” to “actively manage budget parameters on

long-running jobs.”

</point>

</category>

</reference_material>

<important_notes>

The headline story for Opus 4.7 is the jump in real-world agentic

reliability on long-running work, not benchmark gains. The benchmark

deltas are real but incremental; the behavior change partners are

reporting (needs less supervision, self-verifies, keeps going through

tool failures, takes instructions literally) is what actually changes

daily workflows.

The second headline is the vision jump. 2,576px support and the XBOW

visual-acuity result (98.5% vs 54.5%) are a step-function change for any

workflow involving dense visual input - computer-use agents, complex

diagrams, dashboard screenshots, design references.

Frame every improvement in terms of what the user will notice in their

daily work, not benchmark points. “You’ll stop tiling screenshots” beats

“2,576px vision support.” “Your long agent runs will interrupt less” beats

“improved autonomy.”

Opus 4.7 is positioned AGAINST Opus 4.6 (its direct predecessor) and

alongside Mythos Preview (limited release). The “most capable generally

available model” framing is partly because Mythos Preview isn’t broadly

available. This doesn’t invalidate Opus 4.7’s gains, but the marketing

frame deserves to be named honestly.

The literal-instruction-following change is the sneaky one. It’s not

framed as a headline feature, but it breaks existing prompt infrastructure

in ways users won’t notice until their prompts start behaving differently.

This is the migration task most users will miss.

Anchor everything in the user’s specific situation: their tools, their

projects, their Claude Code usage, their content production pipeline,

their infrastructure. The briefing should feel like it was written for

them specifically, not like a personalized-sounding newsletter.

</important_notes>

*This briefing was built for you by Jonathan Edwards - Limited Edition Jonathan on Substack ( co-founder of AI Cred (aicred.ai). Source material comes directly from the official announcement, system card, and benchmarks. Everything below is filtered and interpreted for your specific stack.*

***

I don't have detailed prior context about your specific tools, projects, or workflows from our conversation history — so I'll be upfront about that and cover the highest-leverage points for a technically engaged AI user, flagging where personalization would sharpen this further.

## What This Means for You

The single most consequential behavioral change in Opus 4.7 is literal instruction following. Where Opus 4.6 interpreted prompts loosely, 4.7 executes them precisely as written. If you maintain a `CLAUDE.md` file, saved prompts, agent harnesses, or any reusable prompt library, these need an audit before you trust them on Opus 4.7. Loose language that used to be harmlessly ignored may now over-execute in ways you didn't intend. This isn't framed as a headline feature by Anthropic — which is exactly why it's the change most users will hit without understanding why their prompts are misbehaving.[1]

The agentic reliability upgrade is the actual headline, even if Anthropic buries it in partner quotes. Notion, Ramp, and Warp independently report that Opus 4.7 continues executing through tool failures that used to stop Opus 4.6 cold, and needs less step-by-step supervision on multi-step workflows. If you run Claude Code for extended coding sessions, the category of "hand it off and check back later" expands meaningfully. The model now self-verifies — Vercel specifically flags new behavior where it reasons about correctness before starting work, not just after.[2][3]

Vision is a step-function, not an increment. Image input jumps from ~1.15MP to 3.75MP (2,576px long edge). XBOW's visual-acuity benchmark went from 54.5% on Opus 4.6 to 98.5% on 4.7 — one of the largest single-release jumps in recent memory. If you've ever tiled screenshots, pre-processed diagrams, or downscaled anything to get it under Claude's prior input limits, that workaround is now unnecessary.[4]

## What You'd Otherwise Miss

**The "most capable generally available model" framing is a technicality.** Anthropic positions Opus 4.7 against Mythos Preview, but Mythos Preview is limited-release to select Project Glasswing partners. Calling Opus 4.7 the most capable "generally available" model is almost true by definition — Mythos simply isn't available. This doesn't invalidate Opus 4.7's real gains (SWE-bench Pro jumping from 53.4% to 64.3% is genuine), but the comparative framing deserves the asterisk.[5][6]

**The tokenizer change means your cost math is wrong until you measure it.** Pricing is nominally unchanged at $5/M input, $25/M output  — but Opus 4.7 ships a new tokenizer that inflates token counts by 1.0–1.35x depending on content type. Anthropic says their internal coding evals show net-favorable usage, but they explicitly recommend measuring real traffic. Add to this: Claude Code now defaults to xhigh effort (new tier between `high` and `max`) for all plans. If you're on usage-based billing, your per-session cost is higher by default until you manually dial it back. If you're on a subscription plan, you likely won't pay more nominally but may hit rate limits faster on long agentic runs.[7][1]

**BrowseComp actually regressed.** Opus 4.7 dropped from 83.7% to 79.3% on multi-step web research tasks, now trailing both Gemini 3.1 Pro (85.9%) and GPT-5.4 Pro (89.3%). Anthropic doesn't headline this. If any part of your workflow involves Claude doing multi-step web research or synthesis across sources, this is worth testing directly — 4.7 may underperform 4.6 in that specific mode.[5]

## One More Thing Worth Flagging

The new automatic cyber safeguards  block prohibited security-related requests without prompt negotiation — the workaround is Anthropic's Cyber Verification Program, not creative prompting. If you do any legitimate pen-testing, security research, or even aggressive API fuzzing, expect new refusals that won't respond to reframing. Flag this ahead of time if that work touches your stack.[6]

The hallucination improvement is the one Anthropic claim that partner feedback actually backs up. Vercel specifically called it "noticeably more honest about its own limits." If confident-but-wrong Claude outputs have been a frustration in your workflows, this is the improvement most likely to show up in daily use — fewer confident hallucinations, more "I'm not sure" responses where warranted.[8]

*Ezt a tájékoztatót Jonathan Edwards – Limited Edition Jonathan készítette számodra a Substacken ( az AI Cred (aicred.ai) társalapítója. A forrásanyag közvetlenül a hivatalos bejelentésből, a rendszerkártyából és a benchmarkokból származik. Az alábbiakban minden az egyéni körülményeidre szűrve és értelmezve olvasható.*

***

Nincs részletes előzetes kontextusom a konkrét eszközeidről, projektjeidről vagy munkafolyamataidról a korábbi beszélgetéseinkből – ezt nyíltan elmondom, és a technikailag elkötelezett AI-felhasználók számára legjelentősebb pontokat fedném le, jelezve, hol finomítaná ezt a személyre szabottság.

## Mit jelent ez számodra

Az Opus 4.7 egyetlen legmeghatározóbb viselkedésbeli változása a szó szerinti utasításkövetés. Ahol az Opus 4.6 lazán értelmezte a promptokat, a 4.7 pontosan úgy hajtja végre azokat, ahogy le vannak írva. Ha fenntartasz egy `CLAUDE.md` fájlt, mentett promptokat, ügynökkiosztásokat vagy bármilyen újrafelhasználható promptkönyvtárat, ezeket át kell vizsgálni, mielőtt megbíznál bennük az Opus 4.7 esetén. A korábban ártalmatlanul figyelmen kívül hagyott laza megfogalmazás most nem szándékolt módon túlteljesíthet. Az Anthropic ezt nem vezető funkcióként mutatja be – ami pontosan az oka annak, hogy a legtöbb felhasználó enélkül fog belefutni, értve, miért viselkednek furcsán a promptjaik.[11]

Az ügynöki megbízhatóság fejlesztése a valódi főcím, még ha az Anthropic partneri idézetekben el is ássa. A Notion, a Ramp és a Warp egymástól függetlenül jelenti, hogy az Opus 4.7 folytatja a végrehajtást olyan eszközhibákon keresztül, amelyek korábban megfagyasztották az Opus 4.6-ot, és kevésbé igényel lépésről lépésre való felügyeletet többlépéses munkafolyamatoknál. Ha Claude Code-ot használsz hosszabb kódolási munkamenetekhez, a „add át és nézz vissza később" feladatok kategóriája érdemlegesen bővül. A modell mostantól önellenőriz – a Vercel kifejezetten jelzi az új viselkedést, ahol a munka megkezdése előtt az elvégzés helyességén elmélkedik, nem csak utána.[12][13]

A látásmód egy ugrás, nem egy növekmény. A képbemenet ~1,15 MP-ről 3,75 MP-re ugrik (2 576 px hosszú él). Az XBOW vizuális élességi benchmarkja az Opus 4.6-on mért 54,5%-ról az Opus 4.7-en 98,5%-ra emelkedett – ez az elmúlt évek egyik legnagyobb egyverziós ugrása. Ha valaha is tileoltál képernyőképeket, előfeldolgoztál diagramokat, vagy lekicsinyítettél bármit, hogy az Opus korábbi bemeneti korlátai alá kerüljön, erre a megkerülő megoldásra mostantól nincs szükség.[14]

## Amit egyébként elmulasztanál

**A „legképesebb általánosan elérhető modell" megfogalmazás egy technikai részlet.** Az Anthropic az Opus 4.7-et a Mythos Preview ellen pozicionálja, de a Mythos Preview korlátozott kiadású, csak kiválasztott Project Glasswing partnerek számára elérhető. Az Opus 4.7-et „általánosan elérhetőként" a legképesebbnek nevezni szinte definíciószerűen igaz – a Mythos egyszerűen nem elérhető. Ez nem érvényteleníti az Opus 4.7 valódi eredményeit (az SWE-bench Pro 53,4%-ról 64,3%-ra ugrása valódi), de az összehasonlító keretet megérdemli a csillag.[15][16]

**A tokenizáló változás azt jelenti, hogy a költségszámításod téves, amíg meg nem méred.** Az árazás névlegesen változatlan: 5 $/M bemenet, 25 $/M kimenet  – de az Opus 4.7 egy új tokenizálóval érkezik, amely a tartalom típusától függően 1,0–1,35-szorosára növeli a tokenszámot. Az Anthropic azt mondja, hogy belső kódolási értékeléseik nettó kedvező felhasználást mutatnak, de kifejezetten ajánlják a valós forgalom mérését. Ehhez jön még: a Claude Code mostantól alapértelmezés szerint xhigh erőfeszítési szinten fut (új szint a `high` és a `max` között) minden tervnél. Ha felhasználásalapú számlázáson vagy, a munkamenetenkénti költséged alapértelmezés szerint magasabb, amíg manuálisan vissza nem állítod. Ha előfizetéses terven vagy, névlegesen valószínűleg nem fizetsz többet, de hosszan futó ügynöki munkáknál gyorsabban érheted el a sebességkorlátokat.[17][11]

**A BrowseComp valójában visszaesett.** Az Opus 4.7 a többlépéses webes kutatási feladatokon 83,7%-ról 79,3%-ra csökkent, most elmaradva a Gemini 3.1 Pro (85,9%) és a GPT-5.4 Pro (89,3%) mögött. Az Anthropic ezt nem emeli ki. Ha a munkafolyamatod bármely része magában foglalja, hogy a Claude többlépéses webes kutatást vagy forrásokon átívelő szintézist végez, ezt érdemes közvetlenül tesztelni – a 4.7 ebben a konkrét módban alulteljesíthet a 4.6-hoz képest.[16]

## Még egy dolog, amit érdemes jelezni

Az új automatikus kiberbiztonsági védelem  blokkolja a tiltott biztonsággal kapcsolatos kéréseket prompt-tárgyalás nélkül – a megkerülő megoldás az Anthropic Cyber Verification Programja, nem a kreatív promptolás. Ha végzel jogszerű behatolástesztelést, biztonsági kutatást, vagy akár agresszív API fuzzing-ot, számíts új elutasításokra, amelyek nem reagálnak az átfogalmazásra. Figyelmeztesd magad előre, ha ez a munka érinti a rendszeredet.[15]

A hallucinációk javulása az az egyetlen Anthropic-állítás, amelyet a partneri visszajelzések valóban alátámasztanak. A Vercel kifejezetten „észrevehetően őszintébbnek saját korlátait illetően" nevezte. Ha a magabiztos, de téves Claude-kimenetek frusztrációt okoztak a munkafolyamataidban, ez az a fejlesztés, amely a legvalószínűbben megjelenik a napi használatban – kevesebb magabiztos hallucináció, több „nem vagyok biztos" válasz ott, ahol ez indokolt.[18]
